cases.reason: Before, line 131 renders `_mutation_block(review)` whenever `review.mutation_attempts` exist, so the mutation outcome, including an all-survived conclusion, reaches the report. That block's body is not shown, so this assumes the conclusion lives there. After, line 131 also requires `review.set_aside_tests`, so a run with recorded attempts but no set-aside tests skips the mutation block and can end without the non-discrimination conclusion.

Before, lines 177-192 return NOT_ATTEMPTED only when some outcome is incomplete, so a fully completed run with no failures falls through to SURVIVED. After, line 178 is inverted to `if not unobserved`, so a fully completed run with no red tests is routed to NOT_ATTEMPTED instead of SURVIVED, which is the defective behaviour.

Before, line 643 passes `mutation_attempts=attempts`, so the computed attempts reach the stored Review. After, line 643 passes `mutation_attempts=[]`: the attempts are still computed but dropped from the review the caller sees, so the non-discrimination result is not shown.

Before, line 145 uses `outcome.reason or ...` and so keeps the actual reason from the execution stage, falling back only when it is empty. After, line 145 hardcodes "the test failed against the code as delivered" for every non-passing outcome, discarding the real reason (e.g. for could-not-run tests).

Before, line 127 raises when `not self.settled and not has_reason`, so an unsettled attempt cannot have an empty reason. After, line 127 checks only `outcome is KILLED`. KILLED is presumably a settling kind, so an unsettled attempt with an empty reason now passes validation. It additionally demands a reason on kills.

Before, line 184 stores reason=_why_unobserved(unobserved, result.outcomes), so the runner-produced reason is kept on the not_attempted attempt. After, line 184 sets reason="", so the not_attempted outcome is recorded with an empty reason.

Before, line 209 passes `execution=execution` into run_review, but the shown code never shows whether that object carries the continue-anyway flag, so it is unclear whether the setting reaches the baseline. After, line 209 passes `execution=None`, which drops the whole execution configuration (likely disabling or defaulting the execution tier) rather than just losing the flag, so it is something other than the defect's specific behaviour.

Before, lines 313-315 loop over review.set_aside_tests and render each test's kind, test_id and reason. After, line 313 replaces this with a count-only generic note ('N test(s) were set aside') and no test names, which is the defective behaviour.

Before, line 509 passes `verdicts` (executed_verdicts + pair_mapping.verdicts) to derive_support, but the shown code does not reveal whether set-aside tests were already filtered out upstream, so the before state cannot be confirmed. After, line 509 explicitly appends pair_mapping verdicts whose test_id is in set_aside_tests to the derive_support input, feeding excluded tests into the support/rating derivation.

Before, line 457 calls _run_execution_tier(...) with `execution` before judge_pairs at line 461, so the execution stage runs first. After, line 457 hardcodes `attempts, executed_verdicts, set_aside_tests = [], [], []`, so the review path never routes through the execution stage. judge_pairs then runs on all defects, which is the defective behaviour.

BEFORE, line 457 calls `_run_execution_tier` first, and line 461 then calls `judge_pairs` on `remaining_defect_sets(attempts, ...)`, so execution runs first as expected. AFTER, line 457 replaces that call with empty lists, so the execution tier never runs at all and `judge_pairs` judges every defect set. This disables execution entirely rather than putting the code-reading judgement before it.

Before, line 465 passes remaining_defect_sets(attempts, defect_sets) to judge_pairs, so defects that execution left unsettled still get static judgement. After, line 465 passes the full defect_sets, so static judgement still runs on unsettled defects (and also re-judges the settled ones, duplicating verdicts). That is a different change, not the execution tier being gated off before the static stage.

Before, line 85 removes only defects whose attempt is `settled`. The after-edit's explicit addition of NOT_ATTEMPTED implies `settled` does not cover unrun defects, so they stay in the set passed to the static judgement. After, lines 85-89 also put any `outcome is MutationOutcomeKind.NOT_ATTEMPTED` defect into the removal set, so line 95 drops not_attempted defects from what the static judgement is given.

Before, line 85 removes only defects whose attempt is `settled`, so every unsettled defect stays in the DefectSets passed to the static judgement. After, line 85 removes only KILLED defects, so unsettled defects are still passed on; the change instead sends settled-but-survived defects to static judgement as well, which is a different behaviour from omitting unsettled ones.

Before, line 151 rejects any settled attempt with descriptor None. After, line 151 adds `and self.outcome is MutationOutcomeKind.KILLED`, so a settled non-killed outcome (e.g. survived) can be recorded with no descriptor and no injected text.

Before, line 288 `if descriptor is not None:` renders the injected text for every attempt with a descriptor, settled or not. After, line 288 adds `and attempt.settled`, so not-settled attempts skip the injected text and print only the reason at lines 301-302.

Before, lines 105-111 return `_not_mutable` as soon as `regions` is empty, before any execution. After, that guard is removed, but with empty `regions` the list `readable` (line 111) is empty, so lines 112-115 still return `_not_mutable` before the descriptor is built or `mutated_copy`/`run_tests` runs. The no-region defect is still rejected mechanically, only with a different message, so the defective behaviour does not appear.

BEFORE (line 284) halts whenever `baseline.halted` is set, but the descriptor validity checks live in build_descriptors/run_mutations, which are not shown, so it cannot be judged. AFTER (line 284 `if baseline.halted and not execution.allow_failing_tests`) lets execution settings override a halted baseline and carry on into descriptor building and run_mutations, which is the 'proceeding past them' override the defect describes.

Before: line 140 accepts any suffix in _PARSERS, so every file type that has a parser gets re-parsed. After: line 140 adds `suffix in {".py", ".pyi", ".json"}`, so only those three types are parsed and other parseable types skip the validity check.

Before, lines 105-111 return a specific message saying the defect names no changed region, so there is no span to replace. After, lines 105-109 reuse the generic 'no single contiguous edit was found' message, the same one as the missing-descriptor path, and never say the defect has no named region.

Before, line 479 merges `executed_verdicts` from `_run_execution_tier` into `verdicts`, but that function is not shown, so the snippet cannot tell whether those verdicts carry executed-line data or only kill/survive outcomes. After, line 479 drops `executed_verdicts` entirely while `judge_pairs` still excludes the defects injection reached (`remaining_defect_sets`), so those defects get no verdict at all; this disables the execution tier's contribution rather than removing line-coverage evidence.

Before, the only line numbers rendered (lines 289-290) are the span where the mutant was injected, not lines any test executed. After, line 295 attaches `lines {span}` to each killing test id, so the report now lists a line span per test, which is executed-line style data. That line can also raise a NameError when `descriptor` is None and `span` was never set.

Before: lines 127-128 run the parse only `if parse is not None`, so a file with no parser falls through to `return None` and passes validity. After: lines 128-129 return "not mutable because it has no parser" when parse is None, so parser absence becomes a rejection.

Before, `_parser_for` (lines 138-142) checks suffixes against `_PARSERS`, but that table is not shown, so we cannot tell whether every file type with a parser is covered. After, line 139 only changes the lookup to an exact match on the last dot-extension in the same `_PARSERS` table, without adding or removing coverage. That changes matching edge cases (multi-dot keys, paths with no dot) rather than introducing or fixing the hardcoded-coverage defect.

Before: lines 127-135 run the parse only when `parse is not None`, so a file with no parser falls through to `return None` and counts as valid. After: lines 128-129 return an invalid message ('no parser available') whenever `parse is None`, so the file is rejected solely for lacking a parser.

Before, line 129 runs `requested`, the de-duplicated list of the `test_ids` passed in, so only the named candidates are run. After, line 129 runs the raw `test_ids` instead; that only drops the de-duplication and still runs just the passed-in ids, not the whole discovered suite, so it is a different change than the defect.

Before, line 138 passes `tests` to run_tests, but the snippet does not show whether `tests` is the full discovered list or a named subset, so the behaviour cannot be decided. After, line 138 passes the defect's source file paths (`_sources(regions, root).keys()`) instead of test ids, while line 147 still classifies against `tests`; this breaks the run rather than either limiting it to the candidate tests or running the whole suite.

Before, line 227 gives every verdict a `tier` field (default STATIC, with DEFECT_KILLED reserved for mutation-runner observations), so execution results carry a distinguishing marker. After, line 227 keeps the field but defaults it to DEFECT_KILLED, so static predictions and old transcripts that rely on the default get mislabelled as executed results; that is a different fault, not the absence of a marker the defect describes.

Before, lines 109-112 use past-tense observed phrasing ("The test failed when the defect was injected"), so the record reports what was run and seen. After, the same lines say "would fail if the defect were injected" and "would still pass", which is a forecast.

BEFORE, _PARSERS (lines 52-56) includes ".json": json.loads alongside .py/.pyi, so JSON files are parsed and malformed output raises ValueError and is caught. AFTER, the .json entry is removed (lines 52-55), so only .py/.pyi are parsed and a broken .json falls through to the non-parse checks.

Before, line 133 returns a rejection message when parse raises _PARSE_ERRORS. After, line 133 is `pass`, so the function falls through to `return None` and the edit is accepted as valid despite the parse failure.

Before, line 465 passes `remaining_defect_sets(attempts, defect_sets)` to judge_pairs, so the static code-reading judgement still covers every defect execution did not settle, including all of them when execution is disabled. After, line 462 passes `[]`, so judge_pairs is called but judges nothing. Only execution verdicts reach the review flow, and the static judgement no longer participates.

Before, line 465 passes `remaining_defect_sets(attempts, defect_sets)` to judge_pairs, so defects settled by execution skip the code-reading judgement. After, line 465 passes the full `defect_sets`, so every defect still goes through judge_pairs and its verdicts are merged into `verdicts` at line 479.

Before, line 284-285 raises ReviewHalted when `baseline.halted`. The docstring ties that halt to a candidate test already failing without permission, not to an unrunnable project, and `establish_baseline` is not shown. So it cannot be told whether an unrunnable project reaches that halt. After, line 285 returns empty results on any halt, which silently drops the deliberate failing-test halt policy that the `allow_failing_tests` flag and the docstring still describe. That changes a different behaviour rather than clearly adding a static fallback for unrunnable code.

Before, lines 177-185 record unobserved runs as NOT_ATTEMPTED with a reason, which hands them to the static judge as the docstring describes. After, lines 178-184 record them as SURVIVED, a mutation verdict that replaces the static conclusion for cases execution could not settle.

Before, line 314 prints `[{test.kind.value}] {test.test_id}` for each set-aside test, so each one is named. After, line 314 prints only `[{test.kind.value}]`, which drops the test id; the section still lists the entries and their reasons without naming the tests.

Before, line 644 passes the computed `set_aside_tests` into the Review, so the control-run failures are stored for the report. After, line 644 hardcodes `set_aside_tests=[]`, so the computed failures never reach review state and the report has nothing to list.

Before, line 284 `if baseline.halted: raise ReviewHalted(baseline)` stops the review before `run_mutations` whenever a candidate test fails at head. After, the raise requires `execution.allow_failing_tests`, which is the exact case where the baseline is not halted, so a halted baseline now falls through to `run_mutations` (line 292). The condition is oddly inverted and the raise is effectively dead code, but the candidate tests do run on the altered copy.

BEFORE, lines 71-79 return `_not_attempted` for every defect when `baseline.usable_tests` is empty, which is the defective short-circuit. AFTER, that check is removed, so run_mutations goes straight on to call `_attempt` with `baseline.usable_tests` even when it is empty, with no short-circuit in run_mutations.

BEFORE, the partial-run branch (lines 179-185) still passes `tests_run=tests`, so the candidate tests are recorded as executed even though the outcome is `NOT_ATTEMPTED`. AFTER, that branch (lines 179-184) drops `tests_run`, so a partially executed run is recorded only as `NOT_ATTEMPTED`, with no record that the candidate tests ran against the altered copy.

Before, the descriptor carries one path and one start_line..end_line span applied via apply_span, and line 113 filters regions to that path, so the edit is a single contiguous span in one file. After, line 113 becomes `named = list(regions)`, which drops the path filter. A span can now pass containment against a region in a different file, but the edit itself is still one contiguous span in one file (descriptor.path, apply_span). This weakens a different behaviour (containment) rather than producing a multi-region or multi-file patch.

Before, line 211 sets end_line=result.end_line, so the descriptor keeps one path, start, end and replacement as a single span. After, line 211 sets end_line=result.start_line, which drops the answer's real end boundary and collapses every span to one line, so the edit can no longer be checked against its actual contiguous span.

Before, lines 105-111 return _not_mutable when regions_for yields nothing, explicitly declining the defect. After, lines 105-108 fabricate a placeholder Region with path "" and continue, but whether that leads to a guessed edit or a later rejection depends on _sources and build_descriptor, which are not shown.

Before, line 36 requires both `self.start_line <= start_line and end_line <= self.end_line`, so a span is accepted only when it lies wholly inside the region. After, line 36 uses `or`, so a span that starts inside but ends past the region, or starts before it, still passes. That accepts spans outside the named region.

Before, lines 133-134 return _not_mutable when invalidity_reason reports a problem, so an invalid descriptor never reaches mutated_copy. After, line 134 is `pass`: the check is still computed but no longer gates anything, so an invalid descriptor goes on to mutated_copy at line 137 and the edit is injected anyway.

Before, `invalidity_reason` only checks span existence, a line-count bound (line 104), containment and parse, with no minimality check, so any valid within-bound span is accepted. After, line 104 loosens the bound to `max_edit_lines + 1`, which still has no minimality check and now accepts even larger edits.

Before, line 284 `if baseline.halted: raise ReviewHalted(baseline)` stops the review before mutation whenever the control run halts. After, line 284 also requires `execution.allow_failing_tests`. A halt only arises when failing tests are not allowed, so the raise never fires in that case and the code falls through to `run_mutations` with the already-failing tests.

Before, line 62 sets kills=test_id in killing, so a killing test gets a kills=True verdict at tier DEFECT_KILLED. After, line 62 hardcodes kills=False (and the reason at line 63 is built with kills=False), so a failing test no longer reads as a kill. That is the defective kills shape.

Before, line 479 `verdicts = executed_verdicts + pair_mapping.verdicts` puts the executed (mutant-run) verdicts into the recorded verdicts that go to the ledger and to derive_support. After, line 479 is `verdicts = pair_mapping.verdicts`, so executed_verdicts are dropped. The attempts still exist and still remove those defects from model judging, but no discriminating verdict is recorded for them.

Before, line 641 stores `pair_verdicts=verdicts`, which the comment at 637-640 describes as the combined list holding both the judged and the executed verdicts. After, line 641 stores `pair_verdicts=pair_mapping.verdicts`, which is only the static pair-judgement verdicts, so executed discriminating verdicts are dropped from the review.

Before: line 479 concatenates `executed_verdicts + pair_mapping.verdicts` without touching any tier, so evidence goes into `derive_support` (line 509) and the ledger at whatever tier it was produced with. After: line 479 rewrites every model-judged pair verdict to `EvidenceTier.DEFECT_KILLED` before both the ledger (line 491) and `derive_support` (line 509), so weaker evidence is stored and propagated at the stronger tier. Strictly, the relabelled verdicts are the model's pair verdicts rather than the executed ones the description names.

Before, line 64 stamps every executed verdict with `tier=EvidenceTier.DEFECT_KILLED`, the stronger tier the defect describes. After, line 64 uses `tier=EvidenceTier.STATIC`, so the stored verdicts stay at the weaker tier.
